## 2.1 Summary of sources

\[Fill in one row per source you investigated. Include the ones you rejected in the `Using?` column. This table is the quick reference your reader checks before reading anything else. A clear table will give a reader a good idea of what the focus is beyond the overview.\]

```{r source-summary, echo=FALSE}
sources <- tribble(
  ~Source,            ~Producer,          ~Format,  ~Coverage,          ~Using,
  "[source name]",    "[organization]",   "[CSV]",  "[place, years]",   "Yes",
  "[source name]",    "[organization]",   "[PDF]",  "[place, years]",   "Yes",
  "[source name]",    "[organization]",   "[API]",  "[place, years]",   "No, see 2.4"
)

knitr::kable(sources)
```

## 2.2.1: \[name 1\]

**Producer and authority.** \[Who made this dataset, under what grant, mandate, legal authority, initiative, etc. Ex: If a municipality publishes it, which department, and were they required to? If a researcher published it, what grant was it under? If it's an open source publication from an organization, do they describe why it is published?\]

**Original Dataset Purpose.** \[Why was this collected? The original author likely didn't have the exact same research question as you.\]

**Collection method.** \[How did the values collected get into the file? Sensor, survey, administrative by-product, manual entry, something nobody can tell you? Remember that no answer found is still and answer!\]

**Coverage and resolution.** \[Spatial extent, temporal range, reporting frequency, unit of observation.\]

**Licence.** \[Find the licence declaration and put the shorthand here. If you cannot find it, say here and complete section 3.2.\]

**Access.** \[How you got it, and whether a future user could get it the same way. Include the date you retrieved it if it is from a website, as sometimes web portals or search algorithms can change and make your first search method difficult to replicate.\]

**Known problems.** \[What is wrong with it on a first look-through? Are there any missing years, survey answers, changed definitions, inconsistent identifiers, or NA values, etc. in the dataset?\]

# 3: Licensing and permissions

## 3.1: Licence by source

```{r licence-table, echo=FALSE}
# Note how there is a name in each code block, this 
licences <- tribble(
  ~Source,          ~Licence,                    ~Attribution_required, ~Attribution_given,
  "[source name 1]",  "[e.g. OGL Canada 2.0]",   "Yes",                 "Yes, see below",
  "[source name 2]",  "[licence]",                 "[Yes/No]",            "[Yes/No]"
)

knitr::kable(licences)
```

**Attribution statements.** \[Reproduce the exact attribution each licence requires, aka the wording the licence specifies.\]

## 3.2: Unresolved licensing \[If you were able to find all licencing, delete this\]

\[For any source where you could not determine the licence include: what you tried, who you contacted or what you found, and what you concluded about permissible use based on the project. "Unknown, this is my search or web investigation trail" is worth full marks.\]

## 3.3: Downstream permissions

\[What can someone else do with your data project *output*? If you combine sources under incompatible licences, your merged product may be more restricted than either input was. Work out what licence you can actually offer, and state it. If all open data, state it.\]

# 4: Consent and identifiability

\[If your data does not describe people, say so explicitly and explain why you are confident of that then move on.\]

**Consent.** \[If you collected it: what participants agreed to your survey, and how was their data and consent was recorded. If someone else collected it: what were people told at the time, and does your use fall inside that? If it is your own data, what are you comfortable with people using it for in the future if someone else downloaded it?\]

**Identifiability.** \[How many people are in the smallest reported cell? How small is the population of the place or community you are describing? If it does reference people's data in a public manner (sports stats like goals or time), that is public data. If it is a conversation from a person who did not consent for their interview to be shared, it's not.\]

**How sensitive data will be used.** \[Suppression of identifiable information in your published dataset, aggregation to a coarser unit (bigger groups etc), withholding identifying variables, or a decision not to publish part of the dataset.\]

# 5: Exclusions and harms

## 5.1: Excluded data from the audit

\[Every published dataset will demonstrate what an author aimed to prioritize, and lack of data or missing data can show the same. If you removed a column of the unprocessed dataset, describe what it was, and why you decided to remove it. That could be things like sensitive variables, time periods, places, categories. How could this exclusion affect your data points in your analysis? \]

## 5.2: Who could be harmed

\[Name a plausible misuse and who would be on the receiving end. Think about parties with an interest in the subject you chose, who are not your intended audience.\]

## 5.3: Unreleased working data

\[If there is anything in your working data you would not publish, say what it was and why. If there is nothing, describe why it is okay to publish the working / raw dataset.\]

# 6: Data Stewardship

**Where it lives.** \[Repository, platform, or institution. It's okay to be realisitic about the project after this course ends, as a GitHub account you stop paying attention to in January is a real answer.\]

**Who maintains it.** \[If nobody, say nobody.\]

**Formats and dependencies.** \[Will your files open in ten years? Consider what could break if someone tried it in 2036. The package versions, data format, API, links to sources etc.\]

**Lifespan.** \[How long is this meaningfully usable before it needs updating or should be retired?\]
